newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Mixed 1996 fortunes for European truck makers.
newsitem.headline: Mixed 1996 fortunes for European truck makers.

text.p: German truck maker Mercedes reported strong 1996 sales on Friday while Sweden's Scania showed increased market share in Western Europe and rival Volvo said its North American sales plunged.
Mercedes-Benz's truck unit boosted its worldwide sales by almost nine percent to 348,200 units last year, helped by the company's light trucks and vans.
Kurt Lauk, chief of the unit, told a news conference the company's sales figure was likely to rise further in 1997 to more than 350,000.

Swedish truck makers Scania and Volvo Trucks both said they gained market shares in Europe in 1996. Despite this, Volvo's global truck deliveries plunged by 17 percent due to much weaker North and South American markets. However, Volvo said it expected stronger 1997 sales worldwide.
The three companies took part in the Brussels trucks show, which opened on Friday.
Scania said its share of the heavy truck market in Western Europe rose to 15.5 percent between January and November 1996 from 14.5 percent a year earlier.

"Our market share is growing in the largest market bloc - Great Britain, Germany and France - which together account for about 60 percent of all heavy trucks registered in Western Europe," said Scania senior vice president Urban Erdtman.
He said Scania, which is not present on the North American market, aimed to increase its shares on those key markets.
Scania also boosted its market share in Brazil, the largest South American market, but its sales fell as the total market shrank by 29 percent.
Erdtman said Scania aimed to expand in eastern Europe, for example in Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. "In the long run it is very important for future volume increases," he said.
Volvo's share of the heavy-duty truck market in Europe rose to 16.8 percent in November from 16.2 percent in 1995.
"This boost in market shares consolidated the Volvo Truck Corporation's position as the second largest manufacturer of heavy-duty trucks in Europe," Volvo said in a statement.
Deliveries in Europe changed little at 35,030 trucks.
Karl-Erik Trogen, president of Volvo Trucks, said he expected the European market to be strong also in 1997 although slightly weaker than in 1996. Competition was also likely to become tougher.
But in North America, deliveries plunged 38 percent to 16,855 trucks, resulting in a lower market share of some nine percent compared with around 12-13 percent in earlier years.
Volvo Trucks was hit by a weaker overall market and tough price competition in North America.
Trogen said he expected the North America market to continue to shrink next year but that Volvo aimed to recover lost market shares.
Volvo Trucks aims to reach break-even in North America by the summer and show a "healthy profitability" in 1998, Trogen told Reuters.

The company introduced its VN-series during the year in the North American market. "The new model has been received well and about 2,500 orders were signed in 1996 of which about 500 units have already been delivered," Volvo said in a statement.
Volvo Trucks expected to return to profit in 1997 in South America.
